string-array.name: preset_lines
string-array.item: The game measures this device as you play and settles the frame rate, the 3D scene and the sun shadows by itself.
30 FPS, a smaller 3D scene and no sun shadows: the least heat and the longest play on a charge.
60 FPS, the 3D scene drawn smaller only while the graphics chip is late, sun shadows where there is room for them.
The screen\'s own rate where this device keeps it, the whole 3D scene at the screen\'s full resolution, sun shadows on; drawn at twice the size once play has shown the graphics chip has the time.
What the Advanced page says, setting by setting.

resources.string: Each setting of a preset by itself: resolution, frame-rate limit, sun shadows, render multiplier, dynamic resolution and the graphics driver. Changing one makes the preset Custom.

Resolution, frame-rate limit and sun shadows can also be changed in the game\'s own menu while you play, and take effect at once. Render multiplier, dynamic resolution and graphics driver take effect the next time the game starts.
The share of the screen\'s pixels the picture is made at; the screen enlarges it. 60 to 75% is close to the console\'s own picture.
Draws everything two or three times wider and taller than the console did, for sharper edges, at two to four times the graphics chip\'s work. Needs the game restarted.

On draws the 3D scene with fewer pixels while the graphics chip is late and whole again afterwards; the HUD and the menus keep theirs. Off always draws it whole; Always smaller always at 70% of its width. Needs the game restarted, and does nothing with a render multiplier above 1x.
The Turnip driver this app carries
The software between the game and the graphics chip. On a Snapdragon the app\'s own is usually quicker and draws what the phone\'s gets wrong. Needs the game restarted.
Puts everything on this page back as a newly installed app has it, and the preset to Automatic.

How soon soldiers, vehicles and props change to their simpler models as they get further away: Reduced at half the console\'s distance, Low at a quarter. Faster wherever many of them are in view. Nothing disappears sooner, and it changes nothing for the other players in a match.
85° is recommended for ultrawide 20:9 mobile displays. (65° was original 16:9 console FOV).
Frame-rate limit: Auto (%1$d, or the fastest this device keeps)
Auto starts at the screen\'s rate and settles on what this device keeps; a number is held whatever happens. Only the rates this screen can show are offered.
Held to %1$d FPS: this is what the device keeps here
Screen held at %1$d Hz by the system: %1$d FPS, not %2$d. See the launcher.
The screen is held at %1$d Hz by the system, so the game will show %1$d frames a second under its FPS limit of %2$d. Set the screen to %2$d Hz in the system\'s display settings.

On an AYN handheld: turn on Settings \u203a Display \u203a Smooth Display, or the refresh rate tile in the quick settings (swipe down from the top). The dual-screen assistant can turn it off again after a restart.
The shadows the sun casts cost a fifth or more of a frame. Auto has them where half a minute of play held its frame rate with room to spare; On keeps them at a lower frame rate; Off never draws them.

Sharpens the picture as it is enlarged to the screen, which gives back some of the detail the enlarging blurs; 80 to 100% is nearest a picture drawn at the screen\'s own size. The game is then shown at the screen\'s full resolution whatever the resolution scale says. It costs a third to half a millisecond of the graphics chip\'s time a frame: a few frames a second where the chip is already at its limit.

A small line in the top corner of the game: frames a second, the time a frame takes, and whether the frame-rate limit, the graphics chip or the processor is what holds the frame rate where it is. Tap it for more. It can also be turned on and off in the game\'s menu.
Texture memory: chosen for this phone
How much the texture cache may hold before it starts letting go of what has not been drawn for a while. Left alone, the runtime picks a figure from the memory this phone has.

Turn this off to ignore controllers entirely. Some phones report an accessory, or their own sensors, as a gamepad with a stick that is not centred, which makes the character walk on its own.
Evens out a finger\'s jitter on glass. Too much and aiming feels like it is on ice.

A controller is attached, so a second player can join: Spec Ops co-op and split-screen multiplayer take a second player through the game\u2019s sign-in screen.\n\nHeads-up: two viewports cost frames. Expect dips below 60 FPS, a hot phone, and fast battery drain — choose the Battery saver or Balanced preset in Settings on weaker devices.

Compiles every recorded pipeline before the title screen instead of warming them up during play. Boot takes minutes on a cold cache and the phone gets warm, but there is almost no in-game shader stutter left afterwards. Off means the quick 2-second boot with background warmup.

Avoids freezes the first time a map is played; some objects may appear a few seconds late while their shaders compile. Off compiles each shader the moment it is first drawn, which can freeze the game briefly.

Help tune the game for your phone?

After each session the app can send a short anonymous report of how well the game ran. Reports from many phones show which settings suit each chip, and the results are public.

A report holds only: the phone model, its chip and board, the graphics chip with its driver's name and version, the Android version, the app and game version, the game, mode and map, the minutes played, the average FPS and the 1%% low, whether the graphics chip or the processor held it back, your graphics settings (preset, scene scale, shadows, FPS limit, multiplier), how hot the phone got, and a random number that changes every month.

Nothing else: no name or account, no IP address kept, no file names, nothing about your disc or game files, no location, no contacts.

It is off unless you say yes. You can change your mind and read every report sent in Settings, Network.
